title: The MQL5 Standard Library Explorer (Part 17): Building a Reusable Portfolio Manager with CArrayObj
text:
You
already separated classification, decision control and execution
inside the EA, but a practical bottleneck remains: the program still treats one symbol at a time. Adding a second instrument quickly multiplies state and checks — separate bar times, magic numbers, failure flags, position checks and event handling — and mixes per-symbol state with MetaTrader 5 event logic. That leads to duplicated code, fragile lifecycle handling (leaks or double deletes), and poor scalability.
This article presents a different approach: encapsulate every symbol-specific state and behavior in an independent CStrategyNode, and let a lightweight CPortfolioManager own and route work to those nodes. CArrayObj (FreeMode(true)) implements a clear ownership contract: allocate an unowned node, Initialize() it, then Add() it (the commit point) so the collection becomes responsible for deletion. A short timer centralizes scheduling while each node keeps its own completed-bar gate and failure state. By the end you will have a practical, testable scaffold for multi-symbol EAs that separates concerns, ensures safe memory ownership, and isolates node failures without duplicating event logic.

Why Object Collections
A multi-symbol EA can be written with separate global variables for EURUSD, GBPUSD, USDJPY, and every other instrument. That approach initially appears simple, but each additional symbol introduces another bar time, signal, magic number, failure state, and position check. The program grows horizontally through duplication rather than structurally through reuse.
The alternative is to describe what one managed symbol needs and instantiate that description several times. In object-oriented terms, the description is a class and each managed symbol is an object. A portfolio manager then needs a container capable of storing pointers to those objects, iterating through them, and releasing them safely.
The Standard Library's
CArrayObj
provides a dynamic array of pointers to CObject and derived classes. It supports insertion, access, deletion, sorting, searching, file operations, and configurable memory management. Part 17 concentrates on the operations required for a safe owning collection: FreeMode(), Add(), At(), Delete(), Total(), and Clear().
Before choosing classes, we can translate the original pain into four requirements. These requirements guide the rest of the implementation and provide the criteria used during testing.

Required property
Implementation boundary

One explicit ownership transfer

The sections that follow implement these boundaries in the same order: node state, collection ownership, completed-bar processing, failure isolation, and host-event routing.
Portfolio Architecture
The implementation is divided into three source files. StrategyNode.mqh contains the state and behavior of one symbol-timeframe identity. PortfolioManager.mqh owns the collection and routes work to every node. ReusablePortfolioManagerEA.mq5 connects the manager to MetaTrader 5 event handlers.

The ownership boundary is more important than the number of classes. The manager creates a node, but the collection owns it only after Add() succeeds. This distinction determines which component must delete the pointer on every failure path.
Understanding CArrayObj Ownership
CArrayObj stores CObject pointers. CStrategyNode therefore inherits from
CObject

The declaration divides the node into three deliberate layers. Identity and configuration remain stable after initialization; runtime fields change as bars and positions evolve; helper methods keep trading mechanics behind the public interface. The numeric signal values also make direction explicit: negative means short, zero means neutral, and positive means long. The manager therefore coordinates nodes through Process(), Shutdown(), and Summary() without manipulating their internal trading state.
CArrayObj enables memory management by default, but the manager states the policy explicitly:
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| Constructor: enables FreeMode ownership of added nodes           |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
CPortfolioManager::
CPortfolioManager
(
void
)
  {
   m_nodes.
FreeMode
(
true
);
   m_cycles=
0
;
   m_failed_cycles=
0
;
  }
FreeMode(true) establishes the destruction policy before the first pointer can enter the collection. It does not allocate or initialize a node; it tells CArrayObj what to do when an owned element is deleted or the array is cleared. Initializing the cycle counters in the same constructor gives the manager one consistent starting state for both ownership and diagnostics.
With FreeMode(true), Delete() releases the removed element and Clear() releases all stored elements. The program must not call delete on a pointer after it has entered the collection. If a newly allocated node fails Initialize() or Add(), it remains unowned. The allocating code must delete it.
Fig. 2. Transformation from duplicated globals to an owned node collection
Building the Strategy Node
Initialize() receives everything needed to make one node independent: symbol, timeframe, magic number, execution permission, signal threshold, risk allocation, stop distance, reward-to-risk ratio, and maximum spread. It selects the symbol in Market Watch and configures a dedicated CTrade object.

Initialize() is transactional with respect to node ownership: the manager either receives an initialized node or deletes the still-unowned allocation. It is not free of terminal side effects. A successful SymbolSelect() call can leave the symbol selected in Market Watch even if a later configuration step fails.
The routine validates scalar settings, stores the node identity, assigns the requested magic number to its CTrade object, and selects a filling policy supported by the symbol. Current MQL5 documentation defines SetTypeFillingBySymbol() as a Boolean operation, so the conditional failure check is intentional. The call to iTime() supplies the initial bar timestamp, but zero remains possible while history is unavailable. A true return therefore confirms node configuration, not complete series readiness; later CopyRates() checks remain the authoritative data gate.
AddNode() may transfer the pointer to CArrayObj only after Initialize() returns true. The host constructs magic numbers from InpBaseMagic and the input-list index, which makes that host-generated sequence reproducible. AddNode() itself rejects duplicate symbol-timeframe identities but does not independently reject a magic number already assigned to another node.
The trading rule is deliberately simple. It measures the return between the two most recently completed bars. A return above the positive threshold produces a long signal, a return below the negative threshold produces a short signal, and movement inside the band remains neutral. This rule makes independent node behavior observable without turning the article into a strategy-optimization study.
Independent Completed-Bar Processing
The host timer may fire every second, but a strategy node should not reevaluate the same completed bar repeatedly. Each node therefore retains its own m_last_bar value. This is necessary because symbols may receive data at different times, and one synchronized symbol must not force another node to pretend that its history is ready.
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| One decision cycle: new bar -> signal -> apply action            |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
bool
CStrategyNode::
Process
(
void
)
  {
if
(!m_initialized || !m_enabled)
return
(
false
);
if
(!
IsNewBar
())
return
(
true
);
if
(!
EvaluateSignal
())
     {
Fail
(
"HISTORY NOT READY"
);
return
(
false
);
     }
ApplySignal
();
return
(
true
);
  }
Process() distinguishes normal inactivity from an operational failure. Returning true when no new bar exists means the node was checked successfully and requires no work. Returning false after EvaluateSignal() fails means a required history read was unavailable, so Fail() records a diagnostic. This distinction lets the manager count failed node-processing attempts without treating every timer event between H1 bars as an error.
EvaluateSignal() requests two completed bars with
CopyRates()
beginning at shift 1. It verifies the copy count and the denominator before calculating the return. If history is temporarily unavailable, only that node reports a failure. ProcessAll() continues to the next element.
Position and Risk Boundaries
The host EA calculates a reproducible magic-number sequence from InpBaseMagic and each input-list position. This is deterministic for that host configuration, but the manager does not enforce global magic-number uniqueness when AddNode() is called from other code. The node selects its own position with
CPositionInfo::SelectByMagic()
. It also scans positions on its symbol and blocks trading when another magic number is found. This conservative rule prevents the portfolio example from modifying trades owned by another EA or a manual process.
InpAllowTrading defaults to false. When it remains false, the complete portfolio continues to load history, detect completed bars, calculate signals, count failures, and update the chart summary without submitting orders.
When trading is enabled, each node calculates volume from its fraction of current equity:
V = (E × R / 100) / ((D / Tₛ) × Tᵥ)
where V is volume in lots, E is account equity in the deposit currency, R is the node risk percentage, D is the stop distance in price units, Tₛ is tick size in price units, and Tᵥ is the reported loss tick value per lot. The formula is an educational estimate. The node rejects zero or invalid tick properties and rounds volume downward to the symbol step, but it does not replace OrderCalcMargin(), portfolio exposure checks, or instrument-specific validation for every profit currency and contract type.
The node also checks trading permissions (terminal, program, account, and symbol), spread, minimum stops level, filling mode, symbol digits, and the trade-server return code. A signal alone cannot bypass these boundaries.
Building the Portfolio Manager

The manager stores CObject-compatible pointers, but its public methods expose portfolio concepts rather than array mechanics. AddNode() and RemoveNode() control membership, FindNode() resolves symbol-timeframe identity, and ProcessAll() routes work. This boundary prevents the host EA from depending on collection indexes, which may change after an element is deleted, and keeps ownership rules centralized.
FindNode() performs a linear search because the initial portfolio is small and the article benefits from visible logic. At() returns a CObject pointer, which is cast back to CStrategyNode because this manager accepts only that object type. A future heterogeneous plugin framework should introduce explicit type validation before casting.
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| Runs one cycle per node; failures are counted, never propagated  |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
void
CPortfolioManager::
ProcessAll
(
void
)
  {
   m_cycles++;
for
(
int
i=
0
;i<m_nodes.
Total
();i++)
     {
      CStrategyNode *node=(CStrategyNode*)m_nodes.
At
(i);
if
(node==
NULL
)
        {
         m_failed_cycles++;
         continue;
        }
if
(!node.
Process
())
         m_failed_cycles++;
     }
  }
Despite its historical name, m_failed_cycles counts failed node-processing attempts. It does not count failed portfolio cycles, distinct failed symbols, or recovery events. A temporarily unavailable history series can therefore increment the counter several times and later succeed. The loop always advances to the next index, so one failed call does not prevent the manager from invoking later nodes. The counter is diagnostic evidence that failures occurred; it does not by itself prove their cause or successful recovery.
A failed node increments a portfolio diagnostic but does not terminate the loop. This is failure isolation, not failure suppression: each node records the reason in its own status and journal message, while the manager records the number of unsuccessful node cycles.
Transferring Object Ownership
AddNode() is the most important memory-management routine in the article. It rejects duplicate symbol-timeframe identities, allocates a node, initializes it, and then transfers the pointer to CArrayObj.
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| Creates, initializes, and stores one node; rejects duplicates    |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+

CPortfolioManager::
AddNode

const
string

ENUM_TIMEFRAMES

(

     }

   CStrategyNode *node=
new
CStrategyNode;

(node==

AddNode() forms a three-stage transaction: allocate, initialize, and insert. Ownership remains local during the first two stages, so either failure branch must delete the pointer. The successful Add() call is the commit point. From then onward, deletion must pass through CArrayObj. Keeping that boundary explicit prevents both leaks before insertion and double deletion after insertion.
Before the final Add(), node is locally owned and both failure branches delete it. After Add() succeeds, m_nodes owns the pointer. In the complete attachment, RemoveNode() calls Delete(), while the manager's Shutdown() first invokes each node's Shutdown() and then calls Clear(). With FreeMode enabled, Delete() and Clear() destroy their affected objects.
This division avoids double deletion: the manager may request node-level shutdown, but it does not directly delete a pointer already owned by CArrayObj. The source establishes that intended path. A dedicated destruction log or memory-analysis run would still be required to turn the ownership explanation into runtime evidence for removal, append failure, and full shutdown.
Timer-Driven Event Routing
A chart's OnTick event is driven by its attached symbol. That is an incomplete trigger for a portfolio because another managed symbol may update while the host chart is quiet. The EA therefore creates a timer and routes
OnTimer()
to ProcessAll(). The timer makes processing calls independent of host-chart ticks; it does not guarantee synchronized history, current quotes, or ready series for every managed instrument.
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| Routes each timer event through one portfolio-wide cycle         |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
void
OnTimer
(
void
)
  {
   g_portfolio.
ProcessAll
();
Comment
(g_portfolio.
Summary
());
  }
OnTimer() remains deliberately small because event routing is not portfolio logic. It asks the manager to attempt one pass over the collection and then publishes the resulting snapshot with Comment(). Position refreshes still arrive through the trade-transaction path, while each node controls its own completed-bar gate. This separation lets us change the timer interval or chart presentation without rewriting signal evaluation or ownership behavior.
MetaTrader 5 maintains one timer per program. When a timer event is already queued or being processed, another timer event is not added to that program's queue. Every node still needs its own completed-bar gate because the timer interval is much shorter than the strategy timeframe.
OnTradeTransaction()
asks all nodes to refresh their position view after terminal trading activity. OnDeinit() kills the timer before clearing the collection, ensuring no new portfolio cycle is requested during shutdown.
Operating the Expert Advisor
Download MQL5.zip, open the terminal's Data Folder, and extract the archive there. Merge the archive's top-level MQL5 folder with the existing MQL5 folder. This places ReusablePortfolioManagerEA.mq5 under MQL5\Experts\StandardLibraryExplorer\Part17\ and places PortfolioManager.mqh and StrategyNode.mqh under MQL5\Include\StandardLibraryExplorer\Part17\. The EA imports the manager through <StandardLibraryExplorer\Part17\PortfolioManager.mqh>. Compile ReusablePortfolioManagerEA.mq5 in MetaEditor, then attach it to any chart. The attached chart supplies the program instance, while InpSymbols defines the managed portfolio.

Fig. 3. Multi-symbol positions during the trade-enabled test
Figure 3 records the trade-enabled test during Strategy Tester visualization. The chart comment shows four configured symbol-timeframe nodes. EURUSD, GBPUSD, and AUDUSD each hold a BUY position, while USDJPY remains without a position. The separate symbol tabs show that the host EA is coordinating several markets from one program instance.
The current signal for every node is NEUTRAL, yet three earlier BUY positions remain open. This observation is consistent with ApplySignal(), where a neutral state blocks a new entry without automatically closing an existing position. The visible volume, stop loss, take profit, and “Portfolio node” comments show that the test reached multi-symbol execution. A single frame cannot prove magic-number uniqueness, ownership isolation, risk-sizing accuracy, event-routing correctness, or profitability; those properties require logs and targeted scenarios.
Testing
Results and Remaining Checks
I compiled the three Part 17 source files successfully in MetaTrader 5 Build 6140. I then separated testing into monitoring and execution runs so that the master permission gate could be verified independently from the strategy behavior.

Trade-Enabled Execution Run
For the second run, I set InpAllowTrading=true. Figure 3 shows open BUY positions on three managed symbols while USDJPY remains flat. This is evidence that one EA instance reached multi-symbol execution. It does not, by itself, verify risk calculations, magic-number uniqueness, foreign-position protection, or node recovery. Those claims remain separate test objectives.

Record the MetaTrader 5 build and the full test context: broker symbols, margin mode, host chart, timeframe, interval, modeling mode, spread, commission, slippage, and inputs. Multi-symbol Strategy Tester runs require synchronized history for every requested symbol. The test should separate lifecycle correctness from profitability.
Limitations
The momentum rule is an architectural demonstrator, not evidence of a trading advantage. It uses two completed bars and does not include confirmation, regime classification, or a portfolio-level exposure cap. The shared absolute return threshold also has different economic and volatility meanings across EURUSD, USDJPY, and other instruments.
Every node receives the same timeframe and risk percentage. A four-node portfolio can therefore request up to four times the per-node allocation when signals appear together. Part 19 of the planned roadmap will introduce a portfolio risk manager that considers aggregate exposure before individual nodes submit orders.
The common stop distance is expressed in symbol points. Equal point counts do not imply equal volatility distance across instruments. Although the volume estimate uses tick size and tick value, production sizing should validate broker properties and margin requirements for each instrument and account.
FindNode() uses linear search and the collection is homogeneous by convention. These choices are appropriate for a small educational portfolio. Larger plugin-based systems can implement comparison, sorting, typed wrappers, and indexed lookup.
The conservative foreign-position rule blocks a node whenever another strategy owns a position on the same symbol. This protects netting accounts but may be stricter than necessary on hedging accounts. A later trade-reconciliation module can distinguish tickets and ownership more precisely.
Timer-driven routing removes dependence on host-chart ticks, but it does not make every series ready. Nodes must continue treating zero timestamps, incomplete CopyRates() results, absent quotes, and trade-session restrictions as temporary or terminal conditions.
The current host refreshes position state after initialization and after trade transactions, but the article does not include a dedicated launch-with-existing-positions result. Test that scenario before relying on startup synchronization in a live portfolio.
Conclusion
We moved from a single-symbol EA to a reusable portfolio infrastructure that makes the desired guarantees explicit. CStrategyNode encapsulates all symbol-specific configuration and runtime state (bar gate, signal, magic, trade and position view). CPortfolioManager provides lifecycle coordination only — it does not implement strategy rules — and CArrayObj with FreeMode(true) enforces a predictable ownership boundary: create (local) → Initialize() → Add() (commit ownership) → Delete()/Clear() (collection-controlled destruction).
The practical outcomes are concrete and verifiable: a three-file scaffold (host EA + PortfolioManager + StrategyNode) that can create and remove N nodes from an input list, route timer events to ProcessAll(), maintain independent completed-bar gates, count timer cycles and failed node cycles, and prevent double deletions or leaks. Key operational checks are: nodes initialized, timer cycles incrementing, failed_cycles reflecting transient history or permission failures (not whole-program crashes), trading disabled when InpAllowTrading=false, and proper shutdown (timer stopped then Clear()).
This structure is ready to extend: add indicator caching, portfolio-level risk aggregation, trade reconciliation, and persistent recovery — but always preserve the ownership boundary and test lifecycle correctness independently from any claim of profitability.
Key Lessons
One strategy object can replace a repeated set of symbol-specific globals.
CArrayObj can own objects derived from CObject and release them through FreeMode.
Ownership transfers only after Add() succeeds.
Each symbol-timeframe node needs an independent completed-bar gate and failure state.
A timer triggers portfolio passes independently of host-chart ticks, but it does not guarantee series readiness.
A reproducible host-generated magic sequence is not the same as manager-enforced global uniqueness.
Symbol and magic-number checks protect positions from unrelated strategies.
Monitoring should remain useful when trading permission is disabled.

for: The trading rule is deliberately simple. It measures the return between the two most recently completed bars. A return above the positive threshold produces a long signal, a return below the negative threshold produces a short signal, and movement inside the band remains neutral.
InpSignalThreshold=0.00050 (Closed-bar return threshold) — a concrete, numeric, configurable parameter used in signal evaluation.
EvaluateSignal() requests two completed bars with CopyRates() beginning at shift 1. It verifies the copy count and the denominator before calculating the return.
The formula for volume calculation is explicitly given: V = (E × R / 100) / ((D / Tₛ) × Tᵥ), with defined variables and constraints — enabling deterministic backtesting of position sizing.
The node rejects zero or invalid tick properties and rounds volume downward to the symbol step — a testable implementation detail affecting trade execution.
